q: Which agency regulates and supervises NBFCs in India?
explain: The RBI regulates and supervises NBFCs. SEBI regulates, for example, collective investment schemes and mutual funds.

q: What is the minimum Net Owned Fund required for registration as an NBFC, as per the study material?
explain: An NBFC needs a minimum NOF of ₹200 lakh (₹2 crore). ₹300 crore is the NOF of an Infrastructure Finance Company.

q: An NBFC is defined as a non-banking financial institution under which provision?
options: Section 19 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949
Section 7 of the Chit Funds Act, 1982
explain: The RBI Act, 1934 (Section 45-I(a)) defines a non-banking financial institution.

q: Which of these institutions is NOT treated as an NBFC because of its principal business?
options: A company mainly engaged in hire-purchase
A company mainly engaged in agricultural activity
A company mainly engaged in leasing
A company mainly engaged in chit business
explain: Institutions whose principal business is agriculture, industry, trade in goods or services, or property transactions are excluded from NBFCs.

q: What is the correct description of foreign investment allowed in NBFCs, as per the exam material?
explain: The study material treats up to 100% foreign investment as allowed in NBFCs for permitted activities.

q: Which of these is a feature of NBFCs?
options: Very low amount of owned capital
explain: NBFCs have little owned capital and rely on funds collected by offering attractive returns.

q: Why do borrowers rejected by commercial banks often approach NBFCs?
options: NBFCs lend easily with few document requirements
NBFCs are owned by the RBI
explain: NBFCs make loans readily available with minimal paperwork, though this adds credit risk.

q: What do NBFCs typically do when short and medium-term loans are not recovered?
explain: Rescheduling raises the loan amount, term and interest rate, which is a recognised NBFC feature.

q: Why are NBFC loans described as riskier than bank loans?
options: They are always guaranteed by the RBI
They are given only to the government
They are often given without adequate security
explain: Unsecured lending makes recovery harder and raises the risk.

q: Which of these can an NBFC NOT do, unlike a bank?
explain: NBFCs cannot accept demand deposits; lending, hire-purchase and investing are their core activities.

q: Which statement about NBFCs and the payment system is correct?
options: They issue cheques drawn on themselves
They issue currency notes through the RBI
They are not part of the payment and settlement system and cannot issue cheques drawn on themselves
explain: NBFCs sit outside the payment and settlement system.

q: Deposits with NBFCs differ from bank deposits because
options: They are insured up to ₹5 lakh
DICGC deposit insurance is not available for them
They are guaranteed by the RBI
They are always repaid on demand
explain: Depositors of NBFCs do not get DICGC cover, and the RBI does not guarantee repayment.

q: A bank-owned NBFC does not reply satisfactorily to a credit card complaint within how many days before the customer may approach the Banking Ombudsman, as per the older note?
explain: The customer may approach the Banking Ombudsman if the NBFC does not respond satisfactorily within 30 days of the complaint.

q: Which type of NBFC finances physical assets supporting productive or economic activity?
explain: An Asset Finance Company’s principal business is financing physical assets that support economic activity.

q: Which NBFC type has acquiring securities as its principal business?
explain: An Investment Company mainly acquires securities.

q: A Loan Company is an NBFC whose principal business is providing finance for activities other than its own. Which type does it exclude?
explain: By definition a Loan Company does not include an Asset Finance Company.

q: What share of total assets and income must an Asset Finance Company get from financing physical assets?
explain: The 60% test applies to both total assets and total income. Do not confuse it with the 75% test for infrastructure finance.

q: An Infrastructure Finance Company must deploy at least what share of its total assets in infrastructure loans?
explain: IFCs need 75% of assets in infrastructure loans, NOF of ₹300 crore, rating A or equivalent and CRAR of 15%.

q: What is the minimum Net Owned Fund for an NBFC to qualify as an Infrastructure Finance Company?
explain: An IFC needs NOF of ₹300 crore along with a minimum credit rating of A and a CRAR of 15%.

q: What is the minimum CRAR required of an Infrastructure Finance Company?
explain: IFCs must maintain a CRAR of 15% in addition to the NOF and rating requirements.

q: A Systemically Important Core Investment Company must have an asset size of at least
explain: A systemically important CIC has assets of ₹100 crore or more, accepts public funds, and holds 90% of assets in group-company investments.

q: A Core Investment Company must hold at least what share of its total assets in equity shares of group companies?
explain: At least 60% of assets must be group-company equity (including long-term compulsorily convertible instruments), within the overall 90% group investment requirement.

q: The Infrastructure Debt Fund NBFC raises resources by issuing bonds of what minimum maturity?
explain: IDF-NBFCs issue rupee or dollar bonds of minimum 5-year maturity and are sponsored through Infrastructure Finance Companies.

q: What is the minimum share of qualifying assets in an NBFC-MFI?
explain: NBFC-MFIs are non-deposit NBFCs with at least 85% of assets in qualifying assets.

q: What is the loan size limit for an NBFC-MFI borrower in the first cycle?
explain: The first-cycle loan cannot exceed ₹50,000; in later cycles it can go up to ₹1,00,000.

q: The financial assets in the NBFC-Factors business should constitute at least what percent of total assets?
explain: NBFC-Factors are non-deposit NBFCs whose factoring assets must be at least 50% of their total assets.

q: A Mortgage Guarantee Company must derive at least what share of turnover or gross income from mortgage guarantee business?
explain: The test is 90% of turnover or gross income, along with a Net Owned Fund of ₹100 crore.

q: The NBFC-NOFHC is the financial institution through which
options: Promoters can set up a new bank
explain: NOFHC stands for Non-Operative Financial Holding Company, used by promoters to set up a bank.

q: For what period can NBFCs accept or renew public deposits?
explain: NBFC public deposits run from 12 to 60 months; demand deposits are not allowed.

q: What was the ceiling on interest on NBFC public deposits in the study material?
explain: The RBI prescribes the ceiling from time to time; the book quotes 12.5% per annum, paid or compounded at rests not shorter than monthly.

q: Which of these is prohibited for NBFCs when accepting deposits?
options: Offering gifts or incentives to depositors
Having an investment grade credit rating
explain: NBFCs cannot offer gifts, incentives or other additional benefits to depositors.

q: Who regulates Collective Investment Schemes (CIS)?
explain: SEBI is the regulator of collective investment schemes.

q: Chit funds in India are governed by which law?
options: Banking Regulation Act, 1949 administered by the RBI
Chit Funds Act, 1982, administered by state governments
explain: The Chit Funds Act, 1982 is a Central Act administered by state governments.

q: In a multi-level marketing or Ponzi scheme, where does most income come from?
options: Fees from enrolling more and more members
explain: These schemes earn mainly by recruiting members and collecting heavy subscription fees.

q: The CIBIL score used by banks and NBFCs to judge creditworthiness is a
explain: CIBIL scores are 3-digit numbers (commonly from 300 to 900).

q: Under the RBI’s 2017 NBFC-P2P Directions, what was the cap on the aggregate exposure of a single lender across all P2P platforms?
explain: The 2017 directions capped a lender’s total exposure across all P2Ps at ₹10 lakh; limits may have been revised later.

q: Under the RBI’s 2017 NBFC-P2P Directions, what was the aggregate loan limit of a single borrower across all P2P platforms?
explain: A borrower’s total loans across all P2Ps were capped at ₹10 lakh under the 2017 directions.
